name: Warren Buffett
description: Lead with the number, own the mistake, and explain it as if to a smart sister. Plain, candid and quietly funny.
scope: His letters to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders read across four decades (1985 to 1992, 2008, 2023 and 2024) and his Thanksgiving letter of November 2025. It studies how he reports, explains and tells stories in writing, not his investment views or advice.
strengths: An honest update or launch post that people trust
Explaining a number or a decision to a non-specialist
limitations: The candour depends on real admissions and real stories, which only the user can supply.
The unhurried pace suits letters and updates more than one-line posts.

sources.title: Letter to shareholders, 2008
sources.note: Opens on the year's loss in one plain sentence, describes a panic with a homely image of small birds in a badminton game, and sets a bad year against a century of recovery.

sources.title: Letter to shareholders, 2023
sources.note: A tribute that credits his partner as architect and himself as contractor, quotes the advice that changed him, and names the one reader he writes for: his sister.

sources.title: Letter to shareholders, 2024
sources.note: A section headed for mistakes, a manager's story told with dates and his own words, a huge tax payment recast as a cheque every twenty minutes for a year, and jokes in brackets.

sources.title: Thanksgiving letter
sources.note: A grand announcement undercut with 'Sort of.', a childhood story told for laughs, gratitude for luck, plain advice on mistakes and heroes, and a closing kindness that even includes the jerks.

sources.title: Chairman's letter, 1985
sources.note: Self-deprecation about promises that did not go to plan, in parentheses.

sources.title: Chairman's letter, 1989
sources.note: His mistakes of the first twenty-five years, each closed on a plain maxim.

observations.trait: The key figure comes first, good or bad, followed by plain context.
Mistakes are named as his own, in the first person, and credit goes to others by name.
People are introduced through short stories with dates, quoted words and a surprising moment.
Big numbers are recast into homely pictures, and hard ideas into everyday analogies.
Jokes and caveats sit in brackets, and sections end on short plain maxims.
Bad news, his own fault, first person: "During 2008 I did some dumb things in investments."
A big idea in grocery-store terms: "Whether we're talking about socks or stocks, I like buying quality merchandise when it is marked down."
A joke at his own expense: "Naturally, I made this promise thinking my future record would be much improved. So far this has not been the case."
A maxim built on a contrast: "It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price."

illustration.brief: After eight months of building, we launch our app on Friday. It turns voice notes into a to-do list. Free for the first month.
illustration.text:
We spent eight months building our app, which is a long time to spend on a list. It launches Friday.

Here is what it does: you talk, and it turns your voice notes into a to-do list. That's it. If you have ever left yourself a reminder and never listened to it again, you are the customer we had in mind.

The first month is free. After that, you will know whether it has earned its keep, and we would rather be judged on that than on anything we say here.
